name: Laterex
description: Laterex is a serotonergic-glutamatergic compound that temporarily disrupts the brain's habitual cognitive pathways, forcing neural activity into novel associative routes. The effect is a genuine expansion of lateral thinking — the user doesn't think harder, they think differently, generating connections and solutions that would never emerge through direct cognitive effort. Helix markets it to design firms, creative studios, and R&D departments as a structured creativity tool.
effects: Dramatic increase in novel ideation and associative thinking
Reduced cognitive fixation on established solutions
Mild perceptual loosening — the world seems more malleable and open to reinterpretation
side_effects: Difficulty completing linear tasks while active — structured work becomes almost impossible
Ideas generated on Laterex often seem brilliant in the moment and incoherent in retrospect
Social disinhibition — users say things they wouldn't normally say
Rebound rigidity post-dose — thinking becomes temporarily more locked-in than baseline
cultural_context: Laterex occupies a strange cultural position — it is simultaneously a legitimate corporate tool and a recreational drug with a significant artistic following. Helix leans into this, sponsoring creative events and design competitions where Laterex use is openly acknowledged. In Tier 3 creative industries, using Laterex before a brainstorm session is as normalized as having coffee. On the Shelf, the street version called Sideways is popular among musicians, muralists, and street architects — it's cheap enough to be accessible and the creative effects are genuine even in impure form. The catch is that Sideways has a much rougher dissociative profile.
story_hooks: A Helix-sponsored creative competition has produced a design that the judges cannot explain — it solves a problem in a way that seems to require knowledge the designer shouldn't have, and the designer, heavily dosed during creation, has no memory of how they arrived at it.

A Tier 4 R&D team has been running mandatory Laterex sessions and one of the researchers had a breakthrough that they've now hidden — the idea was too dangerous, too disruptive, and they want to find a way to develop it outside corporate surveillance.

A Shelf artist has been painting murals while on Sideways that appear to contain genuine encoded information — whether they're a courier who doesn't know it, or tapping into something stranger, is unclear.
